a13_0305412ag.text: Okay. The camera's bounced around a little, but we can see the green computer come in every once in a while. [Long pause.]

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Lovell
a13_0305412ag.text: While Jack's getting the sleep station rolled up, I thought I'd show you one interesting corner. We've got a temporary stowage bag here and that's where all our wastepaper and all that goes while we're - after every meal. It's in the right-hand corner down by our dump system.

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Brand
a13_0305412ag.text: Roger. Understand. We're looking at the wastebasket. [Pause.]

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Lovell
a13_0305412ag.text: And the age-old question that's always asked us is how do we get rid of liquid waste and that line that you see, I think you can see it now, it goes right outside where we open up the overboard drain dump, and all of our waste products, liquid waste products, go out through that line and get dumped overboard.

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Brand
a13_0305412ag.text: Roger. Understand, and we can see somebody's foot, as well.

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Lovell
a13_0305412ag.text: Okay. Fred's now going down there, and he is going to try to get underneath the sleep station on his side where we have a sleep restraint. And the whole object of that is to - merely to position the body between the - between the bottom of the spacecraft and - so it doesn't float up between that and the bottom of the couch.

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Brand
a13_0305412ag.text: Roger. The sleep restraint of the hammock is coming into view underneath the couch. It's the white object. [Pause.]

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Lovell
a13_0305412ag.text: You perhaps can see the zipper of the hammock right now. It's the black lines in that white object.

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Brand
a13_0305412ag.text: Right. We can see it.

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Lovell
a13_0305412ag.text: Vance, these hammocks, by the way, are very comfortable. When we first heard about them in the design of Apollo, we thought they weren't necessary, but they turned out to be very nice devices to sleep in. [Long pause.]

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Lovell
a13_0305412ag.text: I'm trying now to get down there with Fred to show you how it works. I keep floating up, though, but maybe we can get a little shot here. [Long pause.]

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Brand
a13_0305412ag.text: Okay. We have somebody upside down in the photograph there now. [Pause.] Realizing, of course, in - in space there is no really right-side up or upside down. It still looks that way to us. [Pause.]

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Lovell
a13_0305412ag.text: Okay. That's - That's Fred now. I'm trying to put him right-side up, for you folks back there in the sleep station. Fred, would you move your hands there so the folks back home can see you?

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Brand
a13_0305412ag.text: Okay. That's coming in real clear, Jim. We see Fred in the sleep restaint - restraint. [Pause.]

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Lovell
a13_0305412ag.text: As a matter of fact, Vance, I find my - I find Fred down there all the time.

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Brand
a13_0305412ag.text: Yeah. I can see he appreciates that. [Pause.] Looks fairly comfortable. [Long pause.]

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Brand
a13_0305412ag.text: Looks like there's a lot of room down there, considering all the boxes on the floor underneath the couch.

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Lovell
a13_0305412ag.text: It's surprising. There still is quite a bit of room down there even with the Hycon camera box down. And right now, I'm going to bring the camera back up. [Long pause.]

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Lovell
a13_0305412ag.text: Okay, Vance. If there is no more that you would like to see right now, we'll terminate our little TV for you today.

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Brand
a13_0305412ag.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Jim. Appreciated seeing inside the spacecraft and getting a look at the Moon that you're rapidly approaching.

a13_0305412ag.speaker: Lovell
a13_0305412ag.text: Roger. This is Odyssey saying goodbye.

a13_0310400.speaker: Brand
a13_0310400.text: Okay. At your convenience we have an item to give you which will have to be copied. It's information on how to photograph Comet Bennett at time 32 hours GET. Over.

a13_0310400.speaker: Brand
a13_0310400.text: Okay. Time 32 hours, 00 minutes GET. Instructions at completion of P23, maneuver to following attitude: roll, 101.0; pitch, 090.0; yaw, 000.0. High Gain Antenna angles will be: pitch, minus 23; yaw, 93. Use normal PTC procedures to dampen rates. After vehicle's stable, and before spin-up, take photographs of Comet Bennett. Use the DAC on the sextant with magazine G. That is, very high-speed black-and-white film, right? That's the dim-light film. Take three photos, one each at 5-, 20-, and 60-seconds time exposure. Use Auto optics. Noun 88 values are: R1, plus 34717; R2, minus 08028; R3, plus 3

a13_0310400.speaker: Haise
a13_0310400.text: Okay. The time is - The event will be at 32:00; and we're to maneuver to the following attitude; roll, 101.0; pitch, 090.0; yaw, all zips. High Gain angles will be pitch, minus 23; yaw, 93. And we're to use normal PTC procedures to damp the rates. And after damping the rates and before spin-up, we're to put the DAC on the sextant with the magazine G, very high-speed black and white film. Then, we're to take three photos, one each at 5-, 20-, and 60-seconds' time exposure using audio - Auto optics. Our Noun 88 values: R1, plus 34717; R2, minus 08028; R3, plus 35075. Thence, three more photos, o

a13_0312014ag.speaker: Brand
a13_0312014ag.text: Jim, for PTC tonight, request that you disable quads C and D. That's the opposite of last night. Over. [Pause.]

a13_0312014ag.speaker: Lovell
a13_0312014ag.text: Okay. For PTC tonight, disable quads C and D.

a13_0312014ag.speaker: Brand
a13_0312014ag.text: Rog. And advise in approximately an hour, we'll have some read-ups whenever you're ready to take them regarding solo book changes.

a13_0312014ag.speaker: Lovell
a13_0312014ag.text: Okay. We'll be standing by for it.

a13_0313052ag.speaker: Haise
a13_0313052ag.text: Have you all got a chance to look at the data on the SPS yet?

a13_0313052ag.speaker: Brand
a13_0313052ag.text: Fred, it looks good, but they haven't had a chance to evaluate everything. They'll probably be finished with looking at strip charts in about 15 minutes, and after that we'll try to get back with you.

a13_0464318.speaker: Lovell
a13_0464318.text: Ah so. Just thought we'd wake you up. And we're awake and getting the spacecraft shipshape. [Garbled]

a13_0464318.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0464318.text: Rog. The spacecraft's in real good shape as far as we're concerned, Jim. We're bored to tears down here. We do have a few little items for you, like a P37 update and a couple of Flight Plan updates. But there's no rush about them. Over.

a13_0464318.speaker: Lovell
a13_0464318.text: Okay. Think about giving us a few minutes. We're breaking out some food, and we'll copy them then.

a13_0464318.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0464318.text: Okay. And the Surgeon will be ready for your sleep report whenever you get that together.

a13_0464318.speaker: Lovell
a13_0464318.text: Righto. If he's listening, LMP had a solid 9 hours of sleep; I couldn't wake him up this morning. The CMP had 6 hours, and the Commander about 5 intermittent.

a13_0464318.speaker: Lovell
a13_0464318.text: Jack's dosimeter - Jack's dosimeter is reading 02026.

a13_0464318.speaker: Lovell
a13_0464318.text: It might be interesting that just after we went to sleep last night we had a Master Alarm and it really scared us. And we were all over the cockpit like a wet noodle.

a13_0464318.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0464318.text: [Laughter] Sorry it wasn't something more significant. I've also got a procedure for you on that H 2 tank; simple thing after you get done stirring up the cryos.

a13_0464656.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0464656.text: That was beautiful. What was it?

a13_0464656.speaker: Lovell
a13_0464656.text: A little of 'With Their Eyes on the Stars' to wake up to.

a13_0464656.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0464656.text: Sounds like all the comforts of home. Have you guys got a flower on your breakfast table?

a13_0465000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0465000-pao.text: This is Apollo Control at 46 hours, 43 minutes. Spacecraft Commander Jim Lovell has just put in a call to us 16 minutes prior to wake up time. Here's that conversation.

a13_0465000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0465000-pao.text: The CapCom is astronaut Joe Kerwin. With him at his console is the backup crew commander John Young.

a13_0465000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0465000-pao.text: Apollo 13 is 159,967 nautical miles [296,259 km] from Earth; velocity, 3,649 feet per second [1,112 m/s].

a13_0465000-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0465000-pao.text: The Flight Dynamics Officer has again updated the S-IVB impact time and location. Impact time; 77 hours, 57 minutes, 5 seconds. Coordinates: 1 degree, 54 minutes south; 28 degrees, 47 minutes west.

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Houston, Apollo 13. Over.

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: 13, Houston. Go ahead. [Pause.]

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: 13, this is Houston. Go.

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Roger, Joe. We're standing by for that P37 block data if you have it for us.

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: Okay. Got it right here, Jim, and it follows. This is the P37 PAD for lift-off plus 60. The reason for the update is for weather avoidance in the MPL at 119 hours. It's the same one we passed you yesterday, and it's the same weather, but we still don't expect a problem at the end of the mission. GET I is 060:00; Delta-V T , 6,079; longitude, minus 153; GET 400K, 118:04. Over.

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: Roger. That's correct. I've got a consumables update for you, Jim, if you're ready for that. [Pause.]

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Ready to copy.

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: Okay. As of 47 hours; RCS total, 1,096; quad Alpha, 270; Bravo, 278; Charlie, 270; Delta, 278; and the H 2 - They gave me the H 2 s in percent, 76 percent; and on the O 2 we have 81 percent. However, we show the O 2 tank 2 reading off-scale high now. We're quite sure it's a sensor failure. We'd like you to verify it with your onboard reading.

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Okay. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Joe, we confirm. Our gauge reading is - on the number 2 O 2 tank is reading off-scale high now, but Jack just tells me that it was okay when we first looked at it this morning.

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: We verify that. At 46:45 we had 82 percent and apparently when he stirred the, the cryos, the sensor broke.

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Okay.

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: So it's no problem. You're above nominal on all your consumables. On the H 2 tank problem, we have a procedure that we'd like you to carry out which is simply turning the H 2 tank 2 heaters to Off at this time, and we want to see whether that won't solve the problem of the tank pressure setting off caution and warning. We want to look at it that way for a few hours.

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Okay. You want both H 2 tank 2 heaters to Off. Is that correct?

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: That's negative; just tank 2. We want tank 1 to stay in Auto.

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Okay. Tank 2 heaters Off at this time.

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: Okay. Good deal. That's been the high tank and apparently while waiting for that pressure switch to close, to start the heater cycle, the tank 1 pressure has been dropping even a little bit lower and just setting off caution and warning, so we feel that if we turn off the tank 2 heater and let tank 1 activate the heater cycle, we won't get into the caution and warning range.

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Roger.

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: Okay, Jim. At your convenience we'd like P00 and Accept. We're ready for - to uplink your state vector now since we will not do midcourse 3. Over.

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Roger. You're in P00 and Accept, no midcourse 3, and we're all set for a state vector update and I'll give you the LM/CM Delta-P here shortly.

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: Okay. Good deal. And I have Flight Plan updates for you later, at your convenience. [Long pause.]

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Houston, Apollo 13. The LM/CM Delta-P is 1.0 psi.

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: Copy, 1.0, Jim.

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Houston, 13. I'm about ready for any Flight Plan updates that you have.

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: Okay, 13. To start off with, got a minor procedural change for Jack on his next P52, if he's ready to listen to that.

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Okay. Jack's still off comm. We'll hold off on that a little bit and then we'll pick it up when he gets on comm.

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: Okay; fine. I've got two updates for you, Jim. One is a - is a procedure for looking for Comet Bennett at about 49:45, and I'll wait till Jack gets up before passing you the details on that. The other update is concerned with going into the LM three hours early, and I think Vance mentioned to you last night that this was a possibility, that we'd like to look at the SHe tank pressure early. And since we're not going to do midcourse 3, we'd like LM entry at 55 hours. Is that okay with you?

a13_0473810.speaker: Lovell
a13_0473810.text: Okay. Right, that's fine with us. We'll move up LM entry to 55 hours.

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: Okay. I've got some details on the Flight Plan for you as follows. Of course, since there's no MCC-3, you'll be deleting all the midcourse 3 stuff including the - the P52, which is called out at about 54½, and we'll be slipping that until later, which I'll - which I'll - which I'll tell - which I'll tell you in a minute. Okay. Then you - we want to move the battery charge up three hours to about 52:30. And we want to move the - moving the LM tunnel vent valve to LM/CM Delta-P up three hours to 52:45, and at that point you can simply go to the 57-hour point in the Flight Plan and change

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: 13, Houston. How do you read? [Long pause.]

a13_0473810.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0473810.text: 13, Houston. You back with us?

a13_0474914.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0474914.text: Apollo 13, Houston. Are you back with us?

a13_0474914.speaker: Lovell
a13_0474914.text: We're back with you.

a13_0474914.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0474914.text: Okay. I've gone through the battery charge, the LM vent valve, the fuel cell purge, and then stop PTC at 55 hours, and your roll attitude there will be 285 degrees, which is per the Flight Plan. The High Gain Antenna angles are slightly different, pitch 23 and yaw 267 degrees. The TV pass till 55:30, the standard LM activation except for some special steps we'll give you to take a look at SHe tank pressure, which I don't have yet. Restart PTC at about 56:30 or whenever you're through with the LM activities, and after that, at your convenience, we'd like you to - to do the P52 option 3 that we

a13_0474914.speaker: Lovell
a13_0474914.text: Okay. That last comment was that we'll do the P52 after we start PTC at about 56:30.

a13_0474914.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0474914.text: That's right. Any time after that; it's not time critical. [Pause.]

a13_0474914.speaker: Lovell
a13_0474914.text: Okay. Let's see if I have some of this, Joe. Around 52:30 we're to do the battery charge on Bat - battery B.

a13_0474914.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0474914.text: That's correct.

a13_0474914.speaker: Lovell
a13_0474914.text: And then about 52:40 we're going to do the LM tunnel vent valve, LM/CM Delta-P which has been written up at 55:40.

a13_0474914.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0474914.text: That's correct.

a13_0474914.speaker: Lovell
a13_0474914.text: We're deleting midcourse-3 and we've moved up LM entry to 55 hours. So we'll merely follow all the - We'll follow all the procedure that leads up to LM entry that was originally scheduled for 58.

a13_0474914.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0474914.text: That's correct. You can start at 57 in the Flight Plan; call it 54 hours and press right on. [Long pause.]

a13_0474914.speaker: Lovell
a13_0474914.text: Okay. Then whenever we're finished with the LM, which we anticipate around 56:30, we'll commence PTC and sometime after that we'll do a P52. [Pause.]

a13_0474914.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0474914.text: That's affirmative. Did you copy the new High Gain angles for 55 hours? [Pause.] The ones we had... [Pause.]

a13_0474914.speaker: Lovell
a13_0474914.text: Okay. We're going to stop the PTC for LM entry - we're going to stop the PTC for LM entry at roll 285, and the High Gain angles are pitch 23 and yaw 267.

a13_0474914.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0474914.text: That's correct, Jim. And, 13, Houston. The computer is yours.

a13_0474914.speaker: Lovell
a13_0474914.text: Computer's ours. We're in Block, and exactly when do you want the TV to be cranked up?

a13_0474914.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0474914.text: You can crank it up sometime prior to 55 hours at your convenience just to set it up. We'll be expecting transmission at 55 hours.

a13_0474914.speaker: Lovell
a13_0474914.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a13_0474914.speaker: Lovell
a13_0474914.text: And, Houston, Apollo 13. One thing I missed about the O 2 fuel cell purge and waste and water dump.

a13_0474914.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0474914.text: Roger that. We'd like the O 2 fuel cell purge and waste water dump at 54:50. [Pause.]

a13_0474914.speaker: Lovell
a13_0474914.text: Roger. We'll pick up those items at 54:50. [Long pause.]

a13_0474914.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0474914.text: Apollo 13, Houston.

a13_0474914.speaker: Swigert
a13_0474914.text: Go ahead, Joe.

a13_0474914.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0474914.text: Rog, Jack. One - one thing we'd like to have done sometime soon is to have you cycle the cryo fans in O 2 tank 2 one more time. We'd like to see if we can get that sensor back.

a13_0474914.speaker: Haise
a13_0474914.text: Okay. Going O 2 tank 2 fan on now.

a13_0474914.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0474914.text: Roger.

a13_0475608.speaker: Lovell
a13_0475608.text: Houston, 13.

a13_0475608.speaker: Lovell
a13_0475608.text: We - We have just one question, the LM tunnel vent valve. We're questioning why we're venting until the Delta-P is greater than 1.7 if we're going to open up the tunnel, then pressurize the LM here shortly.

a13_0475608.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0475608.text: Right. Stand by on that. [Long pause.]

a13_0475608.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0475608.text: 13, Houston.

a13_0475608.speaker: Lovell
a13_0475608.text: Go ahead.

a13_0475608.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0475608.text: Roger. The word on that, Jim, is that they want to ensure the proper O 2 concentration in the LM when you get to the surface, and this is a method of doing that by bleeding out additional nitrogen.

a13_0475608.speaker: Lovell
a13_0475608.text: Okay. Thank you. [Pause.]

a13_0475608.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0475608.text: And, 13, Houston. If Jack is up, I'd like to talk to him about the P52, briefly.

a13_0475608.speaker: Lovell
a13_0475608.text: Okay. He's here.

a13_0475608.speaker: Swigert
a13_0475608.text: Go ahead, Joe.

a13_0475608.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0475608.text: Okay, Jack. What they'd like you to do on this P52 at 49 hours, they've been observing a slight jitter in the optics shaft angle of about 0.2 of a degree plus or minus. Before you come out of the Optics zero position, at the start of this P52, they'd like you to just observe the shaft readout, and see if the jitter occurs on your direct readout there, and also they'd like you to briefly call up a Verb 16, Noun 91 so we can look at the shaft and trunnion angles.

a13_0475608.speaker: Swigert
a13_0475608.text: Okay. Let's see if I got it right. On the P52 at 49 hours, before coming out of zero on the Optics, observe the shaft and also call up 16, 91 and let you look at the shaft and trunnion angles to observe a possible jitter. See whether it occurs in the zero position as well as out of zero.

a13_0475608.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0475608.text: Roger, Jack. That's correct; and if you have time, now, I've got a Flight Plan update for you on looking for the Comet Bennett. [Pause.]

a13_0475608.speaker: Swigert
a13_0475608.text: Okay. Stand by one, Joe. And the commander's going off the air briefly.

a13_0475608.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0475608.text: Roger that.

a13_0475608.speaker: Swigert
a13_0475608.text: Okay, Joe. I'm ready to copy the [garble] now.

a13_0475608.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0475608.text: Okay, Jack. I'm going to read it to you, and then add some comments and then we'll talk about it a little. This should occur sometime after 49:30. After the P52 realign at 49 hours, if time permits, we would like the crew to investigate while in PTC if there is a roll angle in which the comet can be observed for photos. If there is, record the optimum roll angle for possible photography, prior to reinitiating PTC at 56:30 or so, whenever the guys are done in the LM, use P52 planet option, and the following half-unit vectors for tracking Comet Bennett at about 49:46. Are you ready to copy half-

a13_0475608.speaker: Swigert
a13_0475608.text: Okay. Go ahead, Joe.

a13_0475608.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0475608.text: Okay. R1, plus 0.34202; R2, minus 0.07374; R3, plus 0.35719. Read back. [Pause.]

a13_0475608.speaker: Swigert
a13_0475608.text: Okay. Copy. R1, plus 0.34202; R2, minus 0.07374; R3, plus 0.35719.

a13_0475608.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0475608.text: Okay. That's correct and the last sentence on the update is that you can expect AOS of the comet at a roll of 45 degrees and LOS at a roll of 155 degrees. Now, the deal here, Jack, according to the plots they showed me is, the comet appears to be about 10 degrees away from the Sun, and due to the geometry of the LM there shadowing the Sun, it would appear that you will be able to see the comet through the sextant without getting Sun shafting between roll angles of about 45 degrees and 75 degrees. It appears that as your roll gets higher than 75 degrees, although the comet is still in the field

a13_0475608.speaker: Swigert
a13_0475608.text: Okay, Joe. Let me give it back to you and see if I've got it here. After the P52, during our PTC you want us to use P52 and observe Bennett's Comet through the sextant; note a roll angle if we can find it visible. It would be visible somewhere between - ideally between 45 and 75 degrees, and we should lose it about 155 roll, and if we do see it, make an observation of whether it is photographable, note the roll angle for photographs to be taken after or prior to the initiation of PTC at 56:30.

a13_0475608.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0475608.text: That's exactly right, Jack.

a13_0475608.speaker: Swigert
a13_0475608.text: Okay. Real fine.

a13_0480620.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0480620.text: We're ready to have to O 2 tank 2 fan off, and thank you.

a13_0480620.speaker: Swigert
a13_0480620.text: Okay. Doesn't look like we got it back, huh?

a13_0490101.speaker: Swigert
a13_0490101.text: Okay, Joe. I've started into P52 here. I've proceeded on option 3, and on the dis - 1520 - 1525 display, I've called up 16 91. I'm going to let you observe and see while the - the shaft angle while the Optics are still in zero.

a13_0490101.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0490101.text: Okay. Roger that, Jack. We're looking at it, and I'll give you a mark as soon as G&C is happy. [Pause.]

a13_0490101.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0490101.text: 13 Houston. Jack, could you give us a readout on your counter now?

a13_0490101.speaker: Swigert
a13_0490101.text: Okay. I'm showing a shaft of 0.2 and a trunnion of 359.92.

a13_0490101.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0490101.text: Roger. Copy that. Is there any jumping around on the shaft?

a13_0490101.speaker: Swigert
a13_0490101.text: You mean on the TPAC readout?

a13_0490101.speaker: Swigert
a13_0490101.text: As a matter of fact, it went from 0.2 to 0.21.

a13_0490101.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0490101.text: Okay. Copy that. Stand by one.

a13_0490101.speaker: Swigert
a13_0490101.text: Okay. Now it went down - It went down as low as 0.15.

a13_0490101.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0490101.text: Jack, Houston. Let us watch that for another minute or so.

a13_0490101.speaker: Swigert
a13_0490101.text: Okay. I'm in no hurry. It looked like it's varying between 0.14 and 0.8 with an occasional spike up to 0.2.

a13_0490400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0490400-pao.text: That was Jack Swigert, Command Module Pilot. He's aligning his spacecraft platform at this time.

a13_0490400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0490400-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. Apollo 13 now 164,602 nautical miles [304,843 km] away from Earth, traveling at a speed of 3,544 feet per second [1,080 m/s].

a13_0490400-pao.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0490400-pao.text: Jack, Houston. Let us watch that for another minute or so.

a13_0490530.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0490530.text: Apollo 13, Houston. You can press on with P52 now. Over.

a13_0490700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0490700-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. In the Mission Control Center, Gene Kranz is taking the reins of the flight control team. He's sporting a flashy white vest in the best traditions of his team color. Joe Kerwin remains on as our Capsule Communicator with the spacecraft. We're at 49 hours, 6 minutes into the flight and Apollo 13 presently 164,698 nautical miles [305,020 km] out from Earth, traveling at a speed of 3,541 feet per second [1,079 m/s]. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0490817.speaker: Swigert
a13_0490817.text: Hey, Houston, are we clear to torque? Are you reading the torqueing angles? [Pause.]

a13_0490817.speaker: Swigert
a13_0490817.text: Okay. Time of torqueing will be 49 hours, 8 minutes, 35 seconds.

a13_0490900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0490900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 49 hours, and 9 minutes now into the flight. The change of shift news conference is still estimated - has an estimated start of 2:30. Meanwhile in Mission Control, Flight Dynamics has updated our S-IVB impact coordinates in time. We're presently looking at coordinates of 2 degrees, 18 minutes south; 28 degrees, 50 - five zero minutes west at a Ground Elapsed Time of 77 hours, 57 minutes, 5 seconds. Apollo 13 is now 164,814 nautical miles [305,236 km] away from Earth, traveling at a speed of 3,539 feet per second [1,079 m/s].

a13_0490900-pao.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0490900-pao.text: Roger. For Jack, we missed the star angle difference on the P52. Could you read us that?

a13_0490900-pao.speaker: Lovell
a13_0490900-pao.text: Rog, Houston. It was all balls.

a13_0490900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0490900-pao.text: That was Jim Lovell, Spacecraft Commander, responding to Joe Kerwin. We are at 49 hours, 11 minutes now into the flight, and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0490900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0490900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. 49 hours, 15 minutes now into the flight. We'll take down our air-to-ground line at this time since the change of shift briefing is now scheduled to begin. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0490900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0490900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control Houston, 49 hours, 32 minutes now since lift-off. Apollo 13 presently 165,573 nautical miles [306,641 km] out from Earth, traveling at a velocity of 3,522 feet per second [1,074 m/s]. Since we took the line down for the change of shift briefing, we've had no voice communications with the crew, however, we will leave the line open at this time and stand by and continue to monitor. At 49 hours, 33 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0490900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0490900-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 49 hours, 35 minutes since lift-off. We're presently looking at the start of LM activation at 55 hours, Ground Elapsed Time, and Goldstone will be feeding the television transmission at that time. Apollo 13 now 165,675 nautical miles [306,830 km] away from Earth, and traveling at a speed of 3,520 feet per second [1,072 m/s]. We are 49 hours, 36 minutes; and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0491013.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0491013.text: Roger. For Jack, we missed the star angle difference on the P52. Could you read us that?

a13_0491013.speaker: Lovell
a13_0491013.text: Rog, Houston. It was all balls.

a13_0494244.speaker: Swigert
a13_0494244.text: Okay, Joe. I got into P52 about 49:34. We loaded the planet - or Bennett Comet vectors into the planet option, and P52 tracked it all the way across except that it was always occulted by the LM, and we're in a roll angle of 155 now.

a13_0494244.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494244.text: Roger. We're copying your roll angles. At what roll angle were you able to start tracking it, Jack? [Pause.]

a13_0494244.speaker: Swigert
a13_0494244.text: Okay. At the time we entered it there, we were about 66 degrees roll, so either we started too late, or maybe somehow we got a wrong calculation on the roll angle.

a13_0494244.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494244.text: Okay. Let me have G&C comment on that. I suspect that the roll angles we gave you were calculated for exactly 90 degrees pitch, and you're probably wobbling enough that they're not exactly correct.

a13_0494244.speaker: Lovell
a13_0494244.text: Yeah, I think you - You probably got the right idea.

a13_0494524.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494524.text: Okay, Jack. Notice you've secured from that, and that was going to be our recommendation, anyway. We're going to have the guys in the back room look at it and see if they can come up with some - with some better numbers based on the cone angle that - that you're traveling through, whether there are any roll angles that - that are available to you. And if there are, and we have time, we might give it another try; if not, we just will forget it.

a13_0494817.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494817.text: Apollo 13, Houston. Over.

a13_0494817.speaker: Swigert
a13_0494817.text: Go ahead, Joe.

a13_0494817.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494817.text: Okay, Jack. I'd like to pass you a switch configuration on the Cryo O 2 tanks and give you the reason. Right now, we'd like you to go to Heaters tank 1, Off; tank 2, Auto, which is the opposite of the way you've got them now. Over.

a13_0494817.speaker: Swigert
a13_0494817.text: Okay. Is this O 2 or H 2 ?

a13_0494817.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494817.text: This is O 2 , and stand by for a minute and we'll have a - Excuse me. This is H 2 , Jack; it's H 2 . [Long pause.]

a13_0494817.speaker: Swigert
a13_0494817.text: [Garble] is Auto, [garble] 2 Off. [Long pause.]

a13_0494817.speaker: Swigert
a13_0494817.text: Okay, Joe. Do we have you back again?

a13_0494817.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494817.text: Okay, Jack. We're getting you back, and I hope you copied my - my correction of my mistake. I'm talking about the H 2 Cryo Tanks. We'd like the tank 1 Heater to Off; tank 2 to Auto. Over.

a13_0494817.speaker: Swigert
a13_0494817.text: Okay. We lost you again. Here's our heater configuration now. H 2 Heaters 1, Off; 2, Auto. Both O 2 Heaters are in Auto. [Long pause.]

a13_0494817.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494817.text: Okay. That's the configuration we want you in, and here's what we're thinking about. When we went to tank 1 Auto, tank 2 Off; we found that the heater cycled at a tank 1 pressure of about 233 psi, which is well above the caution and warning limit, and if we go to that configuration for sleep, we'll keep from getting Caution and Warning lights during the sleep cycle. Okay. In order to do that comfortably, we want to spend the rest of the day using more H 2 out of tank number 2, so as to get an unbalance in favor of tank 1, so at the end of the sleep cycle it'll all come out even. And that's why

a13_0494817.speaker: Lovell
a13_0494817.text: I'll buy that 100 percent.

a13_0494817.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494817.text: Okay. Good deal. One other detail for you, Jack; G&C tells us that the Optics jitter is very similar to what we had on Apollo 12. It's no problem, but when you're not using the Optics, we recommend that you turn the Optics Power switch to Off to guard against a possible degradation as the flight progresses. Over.

a13_0494817.speaker: Swigert
a13_0494817.text: Okay. Will do. [Long pause.]

a13_0494817.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494817.text: Okay. Apollo 13, Houston. I have one more little update for you, and it's another update to the erasable memory onboard crew charts on page G/9-2. Over. [Long pause.]

a13_0494817.speaker: Lovell
a13_0494817.text: Houston, 13. We're ready to copy.

a13_0494817.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494817.text: Okay, Jim. These are gyro compensation terms. They've already been uplinked, and we're just updating your onboard charts now. In column A: number 11, change from 77646 to 00114; number 12, change from 77332 to 77546; number 13, change from 76617 to 77201. Over.

a13_0494817.speaker: Lovell
a13_0494817.text: The changes are as follows, and all in column A: number 12, the new change is 77546; number 11, the new change is 00114; and 13, the new change is 77201. Over.

a13_0494817.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494817.text: Roger. Readback correct.

a13_0494817.speaker: Swigert
a13_0494817.text: And, Joe, do you know - Are you going to try and let us spot the Bennett Comet on this next revolution here? Or do you want me to turn the Optics power off now?

a13_0494817.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494817.text: Stand by one, Jack. Okay, Jack. We don't have confidence in those roll angles yet, so why don't you turn the Optics off, and we'll update you later.

a13_0494817.speaker: Swigert
a13_0494817.text: Okay. Going off now.

a13_0494817.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0494817.text: Roger.

a13_0495600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0495600-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 49 hours, 55 minutes now into the flight. Apollo 13 now 166,341 nautical miles [308,064 km] away from Earth, traveling at a velocity of 3,505 feet per second [1,068 m/s]. What you heard, was a relatively long exchange between capsule communicator Joe Kerwin and both Command Module Pilot Jack Swigert and spacecraft commander Jim Lovell. The Auto and Off heater positions referred to are the switch positions for the H 2 heaters used to control redundant heaters in the two cryogenic hydrogen tanks. We are at 49 hours, 56 minutes into the flight and continuing to

a13_0495600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0495600-pao.text: This is Apollo Control Houston at 50 hours, 09 minutes now into the flight. We presently show Apollo 13 at an altitude of 166,801 nautical miles [308,915 km], now traveling at a speed of 3,495 feet per second [1,065 m/s].

a13_0495600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0495600-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 50 hours, 25 minutes now into the flight. Our display presently shows Apollo 13 at 167,355 nautical miles [309,941 km] away from Earth, and traveling at a speed of 3,483 feet per second [1,062 m/s]. We've had no voice communication with the crew for the past 15 or so minutes, however, we will standby and continue to keep the line open and live. We're at 55 hours, 25 minutes [means 50 hours, 25 minutes] ; and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Apollo 13, Houston.

a13_0502648.speaker: Swigert
a13_0502648.text: Go ahead.

a13_0502648.speaker: Lovell
a13_0502648.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Roger, Jim. If you've got a couple of minutes now, I'd like to read up to you the change to the LM entry procedure that we'd like you to observe at 55 hours, and the rationale for it. Over.

a13_0502648.speaker: Lovell
a13_0502648.text: Okay, Stand by.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Roger. [Pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Lovell
a13_0502648.text: Go ahead, Joe.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. Before you start copying, this procedure is - is basically simply to activate the supercritical helium pressure gauging so that you can read it. And the concern here is lest this supercritical helium pressure reach 1800 psi by 103 hours, at which point we'd be within a possibility of rupturing the burst disk when you activate the DPS. Now, based on the pressure at launch, and based on a nominal rise time of about 6½ psi per hour between then and now, the pressure should read about 710 psi. Stand by, 13, until we get better comm. [Long pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Lovell
a13_0502648.text: Houston, you were cut out. Would you say again about the helium pressure.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Roger. Based on the prelaunch pressure in the SHe tank and the nominal rise time of about 6½ psi per hour, the pressure should be about 710 at 55 hours. Are you reading? Over. [Pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Jim, Houston. Did you read that last?

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay, Joe. I'm on Omni C now. How do you read?

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: 13, Houston. You're loud and clear now. INCO tells me he's having a little problem at Goldstone and wants me to stand by for a minute. [Pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay. How do you read now, Joe? I'm going from Omni C to D now.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: You're still loud and clear on - on D, Fred. Stand by one.

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay. I'll put her back to Omni B if you all want to take command again? [Long pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: And the last thing we heard, Joe, was that the Supercrit should be reading about 710 psi.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. That's the last thing I passed up. And while we're waiting for INCO to decide here, let me continue. The deadband that is considered acceptable is between 660 and 770 psi. In other words, any rise time that'll give you one - a pressure between those two, will keep you below the critical pressure at 103 hours or so. So, we expect it to read in that - in that band and if it does, there will be no problem. If it reads between 770 and 800 psi, we will want you to check the pressure again at about 59 hours, and I'll get the detailed procedures in a minute. If the pressure is equal to or great

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay. How do you read on Omni C, now?

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. You're loud and clear on Omni C. Stand by one while we get INCO synced up. [Pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay. The rest of your update was that it's okay if it is anywhere between 660 and 770 psi. If it's above 770, you're going to ask us to consider going back in at 59 hours and either get PCM going or sit there and give you gauge reading changes on the basis of that. And you said something about an extreme measure; we may have to consider some sort of DPS maneuver.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: That's correct, Fred. We don't have procedures for that yet, and we don't have any real expectation of getting into it. The procedure I'd like to read up to you now is simply the steps required to get the supercritical helium pressure reading, at 55 hours. Over.

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. We're calling this page TLC-1A, step 6, 'Transfer to LM power.'

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: All right. Stand by one, Joe.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. [Pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Swigert
a13_0502648.text: Okay, Joe. He's ready to copy.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. Step 6, 'Transfer to LM power (floodlights blank), Caution Warning Power Caution light, On. Report GET to MCC. Panel 11, Circuit Breaker EPS Translunar Bus Tie, Closed. Circuit breaker panel 16, EPS Translunar Bus Tie, Closed. Circuit breaker panel 11, Lighting Utility, Closed. And activate utility lights.'...

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Stand by, Joe.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: ...Over. And, 13, Houston. Select Omni Bravo, please. [Long pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay, Joe. I've created a new page here called TLC-1A, item 6, Transfer to LM power and the usual check that the floodlight's blank and that I've got the Caution Warning Power light On; I get a GET from Jack, and I will pass that on down to you. Item 7, Circuit Breakers EPS Translunar Bus Tie, panels 11 and 16, Closed. Step 8, circuit breaker lighting and utility on panel 11, Closed, and turn on the utility lights. However, the lighting is such that I don't really need those. They're in stowage, right now, I guess, in the ISA, and I'll probably just leave them there.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. That's optional. The way we have page TLC-1A written, that was all part of step 6. You haven't even gotten to step 7 yet. Step 7 is as follows. [Pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Fred, Houston. Are you with me? [Long pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Apollo 13, Houston. Are you reading me now?

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay. Houston, 13. How do you read?

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: 13, Houston. Loud and clear. What Omni you on now?

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: I'm going to stay Omni B, if you all want to take command back and you can let INCO jockey them around between B and D. And how many steps we got, so I know whether to write big or small here, Joe?

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. We got steps 6 through 12, but step 7 is the same size as 6, and 8 through 12 are short. They're only one line each.

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. Step 7 follows: 'Circuit breaker panel 11, AC Bus B, Helium PQGS Propellant Display, Close. Circuit breaker 11, AC Bus B, Numeric Lighting, Close. Circuit breaker 11, AC Bus B, Bus Tie Inverter 1, Close. Circuit breaker panel 11, EPS Inverter 1, Close. Circuit breaker panel 16, Instrumentation Sig Sensor, Close. Inverter 1'...

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Hold on a minute, Joe.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay.

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: My shorthand is rather poor today. [Long pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay I'm now up to circuit breaker panel 11, Inverter 1, Close.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. Next was 'Circuit breaker panel 16, Instrumentation Sig Sensor, Close. Then Inverter 1, Select. Then Helium Monitor to Supercrit Press. Report Supercrit Press to MCC.' Over.

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Houston, 13. How do you read?

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: 13, Houston. You're coming through. We still have some background noise. Do you want to read back step 7? [Pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Hello, Houston; 13.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: 13, Houston. Go ahead.

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay, Joe. The last thing I got was Helium Monitor to Supercrit Pressure. [Pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. And the last part of step 7 is, 'Report Supercrit Pressure to MCC,' and read back step 7. [Long pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay. Step 7. Circuit breaker panel 11, AC Bus B, Helium PQGS Display, Close. Main - Circuit breaker panel 11, AC Bus B, Numeric Lighting, Close. CD panel 11, AC Bus - Is that AC Bus B? Bus Tie Inverter 1, Close?

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: That's affirmative.

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: And CB - CB EPS Inverter 1, panel 11, Close. CB panel 16, Instrument Signal Sensor, Close. Inverter 1, Select. Helium Monitor to Supercrit Pressure. Report pressure to MSFN.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. That's correct. Now step 8 is, 'On MCC request, perform step 9.' In other words, you wait for us to decide what to do and that's according to the gauge we've already given you. And step 9, I'll give you now, is 'Helium Monitor to Off, Inverter to Off.' Over. [Pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay. Step 8 says, 'Set in an MCC hold.' Step 9 says, 'On MCC's words, Helium Monitor, Off, Inverter, Off.'

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Roger. That's correct. Step 10 is, 'Configure circuit breaker panels per Activation 3 and 4.' [Long pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay. Configure - step 10, 'Configure circuit breakers per Activation pages 3 and 4.'

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Roger. That's correct. Step 11 is, 'Deactivate the utility lights if you activated them,' and step 12 which is the last one is, 'Transfer to CSM power, usual observations, and report time to MCC.' [Long pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay. Step 11, 'Deactivate utility lights.' 12, 'Transfer to CSM power and note the usual observations and report the GET.'

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. That's it. And, of course, Houston will be requesting you to go to step 9 if the pressure is less than 770. If the pressure's between 770 and 800, we will be asking you to do the following, if you're ready to copy. [Pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Stand by. I've got to find some more blank paper.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Yeah. This is going to be page TLC-3, but it's very short. [Long pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay. Go ahead with TLC-3.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Okay. Stand by 10 seconds, Fred. [Long pause.]

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Fred, Houston.

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: All right. Go ahead.

a13_0502648.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0502648.text: Roger. We'll hold off on that. It was a short three-step procedure which said, 'Repeat activation pages 1, 1A, and 2,' but there was another step in it that nobody understands. So, essentially what we'd recommend in that case would be that you repeat the procedure that we just passed up for reading the Supercrit pressure. If we need to, we'll clarify it later on. And that's all we've got.

a13_0502648.speaker: Haise
a13_0502648.text: Okay.

a13_0505100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0505100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 50 hours, 51 minutes now into the flight. We experienced some communications difficulties during that extended conversation. However, that was Joe Kerwin adding to the LM activation procedures for the 55-hour time in the Flight Plan giving steps required to get readings of the supercritical helium pressure in the LM after Jim Lovell and Fred Haise go inside Aquarius. Fred Haise copied that report for Apollo 13. We now show on our displays, Apollo 13 at 168,262 nautical miles [311,621 km] out from Earth and slowing down; traveling at a velocity now of 3,463 fe

a13_0505738.speaker: Lovell
a13_0505738.text: Okay. One thing, Joe; I just want to double check again. All the stuff that normally was going to start at 57 hours, which the first item was pressurize CSM to 5.7 psia, we're going to move that up to 54 now, so we have our LM entry, which was nominally at 58, at 55. Is that correct?

a13_0510300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0510300-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 51 hours, 3 minutes now into the flight. Apollo 13 presently shows an altitude of 168,651 nautical miles [312,342 km] relative to Earth, and traveling at a velocity of 3,455 feet per second [1,053 m/s]. Among those presently at the capsule communicator's console here in Mission Control is Command Module Pilot Ken Mattingly. We're at 51 hours, 4 minutes into the flight and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0510702.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0510702.text: Roger, 13. Because of the O 2 tank 2 quantity sensor drop out, EECOM wants to keep a little closer track of the - of the cryo quantities, and he's going to be asking you to stir all the cryo tanks at slightly more frequent intervals than - than had been planned, and the first time is now, and we will be calling you probably every 5 or 6 hours, except during sleep period and high activity periods. We'd like you to do it now. Over.

a13_0510702.speaker: Kerwin
a13_0510702.text: And, 13, Houston. For your information, a normal 1-minute or so stir will be fine.

a13_0511700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0511700-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 51 hours, 17 minutes now into the flight. We presently show Apollo 13 at a distance of 169,111 nautical miles [313,194 km] out and travelling at a speed of 3,445 feet per second [1,050 m/s]. In the Mission Control Center we're having a change in capsule communicators. Vance Brand has reported in, taking the place of Joe Kerwin. We're at 51 hours, 18 minutes now; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0511700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0511700-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 51 hours, 29 minutes now into the flight. Apollo 13 now 169,526 nautical miles [313,962 km] in altitude and traveling at a velocity of 3,436 feet per second [1,047 m/s]. We've had no communications with the crew of Apollo 13 for about the last 30 minutes. It's very possible that they have also stepped ahead the eat period in their Flight Plan. We'll stand by however and continue to monitor and at 51 hours, 30 minutes into the flight; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0511700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0511700-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; at 52 hours, 7 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 13. Our digital display presently shows the Apollo 13 spacecraft at an altitude of 170,752 nautical miles [316,233 km], continuing to slow down. Now at a speed of 3,410 feet per second [1,039 m/s]. A relatively quiet period here on the second shift that the White Flight Control Team has pulled at this point in time. Most of the flight controllers talking things over with their respective backrooms. We have not had contact with the crew for almost an hour. We'll stand by and continue to monitor. At 52 hours, 7

a13_0520700-pao.speaker: Brand
a13_0520700-pao.text: Jim, just advisory; expect a Caution and Warning on H 2 tank 1 pretty quick. No problem; just warning you about it.

a13_0520700-pao.speaker: Lovell
a13_0520700-pao.text: Okay. A zero pressure light on H 2 tank 1 coming on shortly, huh?

a13_0520742.speaker: Brand
a13_0520742.text: Jim, just advisory; expect a Caution and Warning on H 2 tank 1 pretty quick. No problem; just warning you about it.

a13_0520742.speaker: Lovell
a13_0520742.text: Okay. A zero pressure light on H 2 tank 1 coming on shortly, huh?

a13_0520742.speaker: Lovell
a13_0520742.text: Okay. Well, you were pretty close. It just came on.

a13_0520742.speaker: Lovell
a13_0520742.text: Well, there's - I guess there's all sorts. Could you go to the horse races with me?

a13_0520742.speaker: Brand
a13_0520742.text: I'm sorry; you were garbled. Say again?

a13_0520742.speaker: Lovell
a13_0520742.text: I said I'd like to invite you to the horse races with me.

a13_0520900-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0520900-pao.text: That was Vance Brand with a caution and warning light advisory timed almost to the second. Jim Lovell responded from the spacecraft. We're at 52 hours, 9 minutes into the flight and the show of Apollo 13 at 170,831 nautical miles [316,379 km] above the Earth, travelling at a speed of 3,408 feet per second [1,039 m/s]. Gene Kranz just spoke to the EECOM and said that's pretty lucky, then he said, 'Oh, correction, that's pretty skilful.' We're at 52 hours, 10 minutes into the flight and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0521655.speaker: Haise
a13_0521655.text: Well, it's time for a little grits again here, Vance.

a13_0521655.speaker: Brand
a13_0521655.text: Understand. Some grits, huh? Chow. Bon appetite.

a13_0521800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0521800-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. That was Fred Haise, a native of Mississippi, saying it's time for some grits in here now. Obviously his conversion of, for describing it's mealtime. We're at 52 hours, 18 minutes into the flight and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0521800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0521800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 52 hours, 23 minutes now into the mission. Apollo 13 is presently 171,246 nautical miles [317,148 km] away from Earth. Its present velocity reads 3,399 feet per second [1,036 m/s]. Continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0521800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0521800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 52 hours, 36 minutes into the flight of Apollo 13. The Apollo 13 spacecraft now shows a distance of 171,726 nautical miles [318,036 km] away from Earth traveling at a speed of 3,389 feet per second [1,033 m/s]. We've just received a further update from the Flight Dynamics Officer with regard to predicted time and coordinates for the S-IVB impact. We now read a time of impact of 77 hours, 56 minutes, 45 seconds with coordinates now displayed here in Mission Control of 2 degrees, 33 minutes south; 18 degrees, 18 minutes west. We're at 52 hours, 37 minutes into

a13_0524520.speaker: Brand
a13_0524520.text: Apollo 13, Houston.

a13_0524520.speaker: Lovell
a13_0524520.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a13_0524520.speaker: Brand
a13_0524520.text: Rog. Just expect that same Caution and Warning to come on again. And you want us to keep warning you of that thing? [Pause.]

a13_0524520.speaker: Lovell
a13_0524520.text: Go ahead, Houston.

a13_0524520.speaker: Brand
a13_0524520.text: Roger, Jim. Just expect a Caution and Warning to come on again the same as it did about an hour ago. [Pause.]

a13_0524520.speaker: Lovell
a13_0524520.text: Go ahead, Houston. We've lost [garble].

a13_0524520.speaker: Brand
a13_0524520.text: Roger. How are you reading me now, Jim? [Long pause.]

a13_0524520.speaker: Lovell
a13_0524520.text: Houston, Apollo 13.

a13_0524520.speaker: Brand
a13_0524520.text: 13, Houston. How do you read now?

a13_0524520.speaker: Lovell
a13_0524520.text: Okay. Read you good now. Seems like we've had a little trouble with the comm today.

a13_0524520.speaker: Brand
a13_0524520.text: Yeah. I guess it's partly because you are further out. We just wanted to tell you that you were going to get that Caution Warning that you just got.

a13_0524520.speaker: Lovell
a13_0524520.text: Righto. We just got it.

a13_0524520.speaker: Brand
a13_0524520.text: And I won't bother you with those calls anymore, unless you especially want them.

a13_0524520.speaker: Lovell
a13_0524520.text: That's okay, Vance. You don't have to call us about that, unless it's something serious.

a13_0524520.speaker: Brand
a13_0524520.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a13_0524520.speaker: Haise
a13_0524520.text: We just - we just ate a can of ham salad and that was an experience.

a13_0524520.speaker: Brand
a13_0524520.text: Rog. Copy. [Pause.]

a13_0524520.speaker: Haise
a13_0524520.text: It's really kind of like eating on the fly. Chasing it around. [Pause.]

a13_0524520.speaker: Brand
a13_0524520.text: Right. Copy. [Long pause.]

a13_0524520.speaker: Haise
a13_0524520.text: But good.

a13_0524800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0524800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 52 hours, 48 minutes now into the flight. Spacecraft Apollo 13 now at an altitude of 172,125 nautical miles [318,775 km] and going at a speed of 3,381 feet per second [1,031 m/s]. In that last conversation exchange we heard from both Jim Lovell and then later describing ham salad sandwich was Fred Haise. We're at 52 hours, 49 minutes into the flight and continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0524800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0524800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 53 hours, 8 minutes into the mission. We now show Apollo 13 at a distance of 172,771 nautical miles [319,972 km] and traveling at a rate of speed of 3,367 feet per second [1,026 m/s]. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0531928.speaker: Lovell
a13_0531928.text: Right, we're not doing anything right now, Vance, we're just getting curious, we could start the LM entry procedures, and get everything squared away, and then when the TV comes up at 55 hours, we could just use it for the TV, and we wouldn't be worrying about checking out the SHe tank pressures and everything like that.

a13_0531928.speaker: Brand
a13_0531928.text: Okay, let us mull that one a minute here, and I'll get right back with you.

a13_0532100-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0532100-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 53 hours, 21 minutes into the flight. Apollo 13 now at a distance of 173,207 nautical miles [320,779 km], and proceeding at a speed of 3,358 feet per second [1,024 m/s]. That last report came to us from spacecraft Commander Jim Lovell. There is a discussion here in the Control Center now as to what our response may be. We're at 53 hours, 22 minutes and continuing to monitor; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0532335.speaker: Lovell
a13_0532335.text: Also, Houston, Apollo 13. We'd like to move up the waste water dump and maybe the O 2 fuel cell purge a little bit early, if we could. [Pause.]

a13_0532630.speaker: Brand
a13_0532630.text: Jim, you're clear to go on into the LM, and just advise though that the TV time is still fixed at 55 hours, and - so we'll be standing by to support your entry and we'll get back with you on a minute - in a minute on the O 2 fuel cell purge and the waste water dump.

a13_0532630.speaker: Brand
a13_0532630.text: And also request your LM/CM Delta-P which was on the Flight Plan for 53 hours. What did you vent it down to? Over. [Pause.]

a13_0532630.speaker: Lovell
a13_0532630.text: We have 1.7 now. We vented it down to that figure.

a13_0532630.speaker: Brand
a13_0532630.text: Okay, you vented down to 1.7, and what did it start at?

a13_0532800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0532800-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 53 hours, 28 minutes. There you've heard the response from CapCom Vance Brand clearing the Apollo 13 Commander and Lunar Module Pilot for going into the LM about an hour earlier than had previously been planned. However, the television transmission time will remain unchanged at 55 hours Ground Elapsed Time. We presently show Apollo 13 at an altitude of 173,422 nautical miles [321,177 km] and at a velocity of 3,354 feet per second [1,022 m/s]. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0533432.speaker: Haise
a13_0533432.text: What do you all read for suit pressure down there? [Pause.]

a13_0533600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0533600-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston. So we have Jim Lovell and Fred Haise cleared to go inside Aquarius a bit early and they're proceeding in that direction now. Although Jim Lovell is presently the only astronaut to have taken a second trip atop the Saturn V and is the first of his group to make a second journey to the Moon, this evening will mark his first step inside the Lunar Module in flight. The Apollo 8 crew circled the Moon with the Command and Service Modules only. We'll standby and continue to monitor at 53 hours, 36 minutes into the flight.

a13_0533858.speaker: Lovell
a13_0533858.text: We'd like another confirmation, when we closed the tunnel vent valve back to LM/CM Delta-P, we were reading about 1.7 - 1.75, and it slowly went up now to about - oh, I'd say a little less than 2.2. Seems to be holding there - Is there a lag in the gauging system?

a13_0533858.speaker: Brand
a13_0533858.text: Okay. We'll - we'll ask that question. Stand by.

a13_0534058.speaker: Brand
a13_0534058.text: Okay, to answer your question, Jim, that increase in pressure is normal, because it was just tracking an increase in cabin pressure.

a13_0534058.speaker: Brand
a13_0534058.text: And, 13, from Houston, it's okay with us if you want to move the O 2 fuel cell purge and the waste water dump up to this time. Over.

a13_0534058.speaker: Lovell
a13_0534058.text: Okay. We'll work it in shortly. Thank you.

a13_0534400-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0534400-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 53 hours, 44 minutes into the mission. Apollo 13 at the present time 173,934 nautical miles [322,126 km] out from Earth and now going at a speed of 3,343 feet per second [1,019 m/s]. We're at 53 hours, 44 minutes and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0534511.speaker: Brand
a13_0534511.text: Jim, recommend you stay in the PTC until we stop it for the TV at 55 hours, in case you were thinking of...

a13_0534511.speaker: Brand
a13_0534511.text: Roger. Recommend you continue PTC until 55 hours. Over. [Long pause.]

a13_0534511.speaker: Brand
a13_0534511.text: That's affirm, Jim. How do you read now?

a13_0534511.speaker: Lovell
a13_0534511.text: Okay. We read you loud and clear.

a13_0534511.speaker: Brand
a13_0534511.text: Okay. The only comment that we just made was that, in case you were thinking of stopping PTC, there's no need to stop it until 55 GET when TV starts.

a13_0534511.speaker: Lovell
a13_0534511.text: Right. We'll stop it when we're setting up our TV.

a13_0534600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0534600-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. EECOM confirms to Flight Director Gene Kranz that the fuel cells are being purged and the water dump being accomplished at this time.

a13_0534600-pao.speaker: Brand
a13_0534600-pao.text: That's affirm, Jim. How do you read now?

a13_0534800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0534800-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 53 hours, 48 minutes. EECOM confirms to Flight Director Gene Kranz that the cabin pressures are being equalized now. We presently show Apollo 13 at an altitude of 174,070 nautical miles [322,378 km] and traveling at a speed of 3,340 feet per second [1,018 m/s]. We're at 53 hours, 48 minutes; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0534800-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0534800-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. 53 hours, 51 minutes. EECOM reports the cabin pressures have leveled off now, reading 4.7 - 4.8. We now show Apollo 13 at 174,160 nautical miles [322,544 km] away and going at a speed of 3,338 feet per second [1,017 m/s]. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0535434.speaker: Swigert
a13_0535434.text: Okay, Houston, the waste water dump and O 2 fuel cell purge are complete.

a13_0535500-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0535500-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston; 53 hours, 55 minutes. That was Back-up Commander for Apollo 13, John Young, returning that call from the spacecraft. Capsule communicator Vance Brand has left his console for a brief period of time to attend a meeting on the LM activation procedures and the monitoring of the supercritical helium tank readings. We're at 53 hours 55 minutes and now show Apollo 13 at 174,309 nautical miles and traveling at a rate of speed of 3,500 - correction 3,335 feet per second. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0540554.speaker: Swigert
a13_0540554.text: Okay, Houston, the LM/CM Delta-P is constant. We're going to go ahead with hatch removal.

a13_0540600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0540600-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston. That was Fred Haise telling Houston that they're ready to proceed with hatch opening.

a13_0540600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0540600-pao.text: Apollo 13 apparently mystified for the moment about John Young's voice. We show 13 at an altitude of 174,664 nautical miles [323,478 km] and with a velocity of 3,328 feet per second [1,014 m/s]. We're now at 54 hours, 7 minutes into the flight and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0542415.speaker: Young
a13_0542415.text: This is Houston. Go ahead, 13. [Long pause.]

a13_0542415.speaker: Swigert
a13_0542415.text: Okay. The LMP has entered the LM.

a13_0542415.speaker: Swigert
a13_0542415.text: Thank you. I had a good CDR.

a13_0542415.speaker: Young
a13_0542415.text: You're doing it on your own now.

a13_0542415.speaker: Haise
a13_0542415.text: Yeah, it feels like I'm back at home, again, John, down in here.

a13_0542415.speaker: Swigert
a13_0542415.text: I hope you did a good job, John.

a13_0542415.speaker: Swigert
a13_0542415.text: Okay, Houston, we want to take the FM and bring up TV here for our own use. Then we'll go to Transmit 1 - at 55 hours. [Pause.]

a13_0542600-pao.speaker: Haise
a13_0542600-pao.text: Yeah, it feels like I'm back at home, again, John, down in here.

a13_0542600-pao.speaker: Swigert
a13_0542600-pao.text: I hope you did a good job, John.

a13_0542600-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0542600-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 54 hours, 26 minutes into the flight. That was Jack Swigert reporting that Fred Haise is now inside the Lunar Module. And carrying on a brief discussion with his former spacecraft Commander - his backup Commander - for this mission, John Young. We now show Apollo 13 at an altitude of 175,307 nautical miles [324,669 km].

a13_0542700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0542700-pao.text: Apollo 13 now traveling at a speed of 3,314 feet per second [1,010 m/s]. We're at 54 hours, 27 minutes now into the flight, and this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0542700-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0542700-pao.text: This is Apollo Control, Houston at 54 hours, 42 minutes now into the flight of Apollo 13. Apollo 13 now shows an altitude of 175,826 nautical miles [325,630 km] and its speed reads 3,304 feet per second [1,007 m/s]. Network has been advised by Goldstone that the network does now have the capability of receiving television at any time. We will stand by in the event we should receive an early television transmission. At this point we do not expect to receive such, but we will stand by at 54 hours, 43 minutes into the flight. This is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0544628.speaker: Swigert
a13_0544628.text: Okay, Houston, we've transferred to LM power; the time was 54 hours, 46 minutes, 15 seconds.

a13_0544628.speaker: Lousma
a13_0544628.text: Roger, Jack. Transfer to LM power. Thank you.

a13_0544628.speaker: Haise
a13_0544628.text: And the docking-tunnel index, Jack, was minus 2 degrees.

a13_0544628.speaker: Lousma
a13_0544628.text: Say again, Fred, you're coming in with a lot of background noise.

a13_0544628.speaker: Haise
a13_0544628.text: Okay. The docking-tunnel index mark was minus 2 degrees.

a13_0544917.speaker: Haise
a13_0544917.text: Okay. Jack, how do you read? [Pause.]

a13_0544917.speaker: Lousma
a13_0544917.text: Fred, Houston is reading you loud and clear.

a13_0544917.speaker: Haise
a13_0544917.text: Okay. I've got up through step 7 now, and I'm not getting much of a light in the helium indicator here. Why don't I review for you how we've proceeded, and you look at the procedure you gave me, and see if we've missed anything.

a13_0544917.speaker: Haise
a13_0544917.text: Okay. We transferred to LM power and that looked okay. I'm staring at a Caution and Warning Power light, and all the red flags; and we got both X Lunar Bus Tie breakers, In. The Utility Lighting breaker is In; then AC Bus B Helium PQS Display; the AC Bus B Numeric Lighting, and AC Bus B Inverter 1 is - Bus Tie is Closed. Then I closed the Inverter 1 breaker, and I've selected, on panel 16, and the Signal Consensor [sic] breaker is in; I've selected Inverter 1 and put the Helium Monitor switch to Supercrit and I have no lights. [Pause.]

a13_0544917.speaker: Lousma
a13_0544917.text: Okay, Fred, let us take a look at it.

a13_0544917.speaker: Haise
a13_0544917.text: I was wondering, do we need an A - do we need, possibly, in the - one of the Anun/Dock/Component breakers in?

a13_0544917.speaker: Haise
a13_0544917.text: Okay, Jack. Hold the phone. I forgot the rheostat was cranked all the way down on the Anun/Num and it's showing 720, which looks like a pretty good - pretty good number.

a13_0544917.speaker: Lousma
a13_0544917.text: Roger. We copy 720. Thank you, Fred...

a13_0544917.speaker: Haise
a13_0544917.text: Flashed to 7 - Okay, and it just flickered down to 710. It's kind of flickering between 710 and 720.

a13_0544917.speaker: Lousma
a13_0544917.text: Okay, Fred. Those are good numbers, and we're not going to have to crank up the TM. That's the number we were looking for.

a13_0544917.speaker: Haise
a13_0544917.text: Very good. Okay. Do you want me to back out of this in reverse at least as far as getting this part of it powered down?

a13_0544917.speaker: Lousma
a13_0544917.text: Fred, this is Houston. Go ahead and back out of this little test and proceed.

a13_0545300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0545300-pao.text: You heard that report from Fred Haise.

a13_0545300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0545300-pao.text: Our supercritical helium pressure reading was 720 pounds per square inch. A very desirable number. We're at 54 hours, 53 minutes now into the flight. Apollo 13 at 176,171 nautical miles [326,269 km] away from Earth. We're standing by now for receipt of television.

a13_0545300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0545300-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston; 54 hours, 55 minutes. We repeat that earlier report from LM pilot Fred Haise. He read his supercritical helium pressure at 720 pounds per square inch. Well under the 770 pounds per square inch mark earlier identified as a point for further scrutinization.

a13_0545300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0545300-pao.text: We now show 13 traveling at 3,296 feet per second [1,005 m/s] and at an altitude of 176,240 nautical miles [326,396 km].

a13_0545300-pao.speaker: Mission Control
a13_0545300-pao.text: Apollo Control, Houston at 54 hours, 57 minutes. Jack Lousma is now filling the position of capsule communicator in the Mission Control Center. That was Jack who received that last report from Lunar Module Pilot Fred Haise. Standing by; this is Apollo Control, Houston.

a13_0545901.speaker: Swigert
a13_0545901.text: Okay. We're back on CSM power. The time was 54 hours, 58 minutes, 50 seconds.

a13_0545901.speaker: Swigert
a13_0545901.text: Okay, Houston, we'll try to pick you up on the High Gain.

a13_0545901.speaker: Lousma
a13_0545901.text: And, 13, we're ready on the TV when you are. [Pause.]

a13_0545901.speaker: Lousma
a13_0545901.text: 13, we're ready on the TV when you are. Any time.

a13_0545901.speaker: Lovell
a13_0545901.text: Okay, sounds good. With you in a minute, we're just cranking up High Gain now. [Long pause.]

a13_0545901.speaker: Lovell
a13_0545901.text: Okay, Houston. How do you read us in the High Gain?

a13_0545901.speaker: Lousma
a13_0545901.text: We're hearing you 5 square, Jim, how me?

a13_0545901.speaker: Lousma
a13_0545901.text: As you were on that, Jim. We don't have you on High Gain yet. We're still looking at you. [Long pause.]

a13_0545901.speaker: Lousma
a13_0545901.text: 13, Houston. In this attitude, we'd suggest pitch 5, yaw 237 on the High Gain. Over.

a13_0550512.speaker: Swigert
a13_0550512.text: Okay, Jack. Can you - can you read the High Gain now? [Pause.]

a13_0550512.speaker: Lousma
a13_0550512.text: Affirmative, Jack. We've got you on a High Gain and it appears to us that we're in Wide beam - Wide beam width.

a13_0550512.speaker: Swigert
a13_0550512.text: Yeah. We can't get it to come down to Narrow. We tried to switch to Auto Track or Reacq, and it - yaw drives around from 270 to 0. And pitch goes from about 6 degrees around to 90. I'm trying - we're sitting at manual now at the angles that you gave us, and I'll try and get you in Medium and Narrow beam width picking it up manually here.

a13_0550512.speaker: Lousma
a13_0550512.text: Roger, Jack. Meanwhile, we'll look at the situation you describe there.

a13_0550512.speaker: Swigert
a13_0550512.text: Okay. And it does it on both sets of servo electronic power. [Long pause.]

a13_0550512.speaker: Swigert
a13_0550512.text: Jack, what it looks like is that, when we hit 239 degrees at this attitude, it hit some sort of scan limit or something and drops off. [Pause.]

a13_0550512.speaker: Swigert
a13_0550512.text: Okay, I'm trying you in Wide or Medium beam width now. [Pause.]

a13_0550512.speaker: Swigert
a13_0550512.text: Can you pick up the TV in this condition here at all? [Pause.]

a13_0550512.speaker: Lousma
a13_0550512.text: Negative, Jack. We'll have to have the Narrow beam width.

a13_0550512.speaker: Swigert
a13_0550512.text: Okay. Can you give us, maybe, a slight maneuver? [Long pause.]

a13_0550512.speaker: Lousma
a13_0550512.text: Jack, we'd like you to check two High Gain circuit breakers down in panel 25. Check your High Gain group 2 and your High Gain on the flight bus. Over.

a13_0550512.speaker: Swigert
a13_0550512.text: Okay. Okay, Jack, they're both In.

a13_0550512.speaker: Lousma
a13_0550512.text: 13, we've got an attitude suggestion for you. We suggest that you go to roll 285 and try pitch 90 and yaw 0. Over.

a13_0551400.speaker: Lovell
a13_0551400.text: Okay, Houston; Apollo 13. I think we've got High Gain locked up now. Do you confirm?

a13_0551400.speaker: Lousma
a13_0551400.text: We confirm that, Jim, we've got you locked up on the High Gain and narrow beam.

a13_0551400.speaker: Lovell
a13_0551400.text: Okay, sounds good. We'll get the TV started right away.

a13_0551400.speaker: Lousma
a13_0551400.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a13_0551400.speaker: Lousma
a13_0551400.text: 13, Houston. We'd like to disable Quads C and D; use Alpha and Bravo. Over. [Pause.]

a13_0551400.speaker: Swigert
a13_0551400.text: Okay... [Long pause.]

a13_0551400.speaker: Lovell
a13_0551400.text: ...Disable quads C and D. Roger.

a13_0551400.speaker: Lousma
a13_0551400.text: Okay, 13. We've got Freddo on TV.

a13_0551400.speaker: Lovell
a13_0551400.text: Roger, Houston. What we plan to do for you today is start out in the space shipper [sic] Odyssey, and take you on through from Odyssey in through the tunnel into Aquarius. And show you a little bit of the landing vehicle, and your TV operator is now resting on the center couch, looking at Fred Haise, whose head is now just about at the beginning of the tunnel, and his back is against the Lower Equipment Bay optical area. And Fred will now transport himself into the tunnel, and into the spaceship Aquarius.

a13_0551400.speaker: Haise
a13_0551400.text: You know one thing I noted, Jack, when I first came across here, that starting upright in the Command Module and heading down in Aquarius, there's a little bit of an orientation change that, even though I'd been through it once in the water tank, it still pretty unusual. I find myself, now, standing with my head on the floor when I get down inside the LM. [Pause.]

a13_0551400.speaker: Lousma
a13_0551400.text: That's a great picture, Jim. You got the light just right. [Pause.]

a13_0551400.speaker: Haise
a13_0551400.text: And one of the nice things, Jack, particularly for a novice like myself, is the - the ease of moving around in here. It's, of course, as you know from working in the Command Module Simulator, it's really quite a boon to have zero gravity as an aid. Because you get - pretty confining, really, at one g, to move around very much in there, and it's quite easy in this environment. [Pause.] The LM, as you can see, it looked pretty clean, I found a couple of loose washers about it and the - a little plastic cap off the sequence camera had come loose and I found it lodged over by the ED panel. [Pause.

a13_0551400.speaker: Haise
a13_0551400.text: The second backpack is mounted down on the LM floor, I hope, positioned right between the two of us. I have my hand on it at this time.

a13_0551400.speaker: Lousma
a13_0551400.text: Roger, Fred. We see it. The picture's coming through real good, and your description is good. We see Jim's got the camera oriented the way we like to look at it. So, keep talking. [Pause.]

a13_0551400.speaker: Haise
a13_0551400.text: Okay. I guess everybody has pretty much envisioned the space program as being all a lot of exotic electronics, and, certainly, a lot of it is. But I thought I'd bring out a couple of items here in conjunction with the PLSS. After the first EVA, you get a very accurate measurement of the amount of water that's left in the PLSSs. We're going to make use of this bag I'm showing now to collect the remaining water out of the PLSS and see just how much we really did have left, and hopefully, on future missions, to be able to extend safely the allowable time on these units even a little further. And,

a13_0551400.speaker: Lousma
a13_0551400.text: That'll be the day. [Pause.]

a13_0551400.speaker: Haise
a13_0551400.text: I think even you'd weigh zero here, Jack. [Pause.]

a13_0551400.speaker: Lousma
a13_0551400.text: Touché [Long pause.].

a13_0551400.speaker: Lovell
a13_0551400.text: Houston, this is Jim. Since Fred's been in the Lunar Module, and since he's the Lunar Module Pilot, this is the first time that he's felt that he's been right-side up. [Pause.]

a13_0551400.speaker: Lousma
a13_0551400.text: Roger, Jim.

a13_0551400.speaker: Lovell
a13_0551400.text: I might tell you that we're looking at right now, that round bag that's just behind Fred holds our vacuum hose; and when we get back inside the LM, we'll hook the vacuum off our suits, and it's resting or it's attached to the hatch which will - we will open to go on to the lunar surface, and, of course, to come back in. The hatch which we have come to now is a round hatch, which is our docking hatch between the - between Odyssey and Aquarius.

a13_0551400.speaker: Lousma
a13_0551400.text: Roger, and we see Fred looking in the vacuum cleaner there now. [Pause.]

a13_0551400.speaker: Haise
a13_0551400.text: Okay, what I have out now, Jack, is a LEVA, which has also been shown before. It's a head garment for wearing out on the surface, and I - I'm bringing Jim's out here to show a couple of mods [modifications]. One problem before is that the cast of characters down on the surface haven't been able to be distinguished apart very well. So, not only Jim's suit has some red stripes on it, but as you can see his LEVA also has a - a red stripe. [Long pause.]

a13_0551400.speaker: Haise
a13_0551400.text: And now you can see one other mod too here, Jack, which I hadn't really seen myself before. I guess on 12, Pete and Al had commented about the - commented about having trouble with sunlight in the eyes, so on our LEVAs they put on a new center section which you can pull down and use sort of like a baseball cap.

a13_0551400.speaker: Lovell
a13_0551400.text: Okay, Jack. Who fixed up our LEVAs? [Long pause.]

a13_0551400.speaker: Haise
a13_0551400.text: How's the detail on this one, Jack?

a13_0551400.speaker: Lousma
a13_0551400.text: Say again, Fred.

a13_0551400.speaker: Haise
a13_0551400.text: Can you see any detail in this picture now, or am I blocking out too much of the sunlight?

a13_0551400.speaker: Lousma
a13_0551400.text: That's affirmative. We've got a good picture of the LEVA there, and it's coming through loud and clear.

a13_0551400.speaker: Haise
a13_0551400.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a13_0551400.speaker: Lovell
a13_0551400.text: Okay, Jack, while Fred is putting away my helmet, you're looking over into Fred's station now. How's this picture, is it okay before - or do I have to adjust it?

a13_0551400.speaker: Lousma
a13_0551400.text: We have a hunch that the setting might be in Peak but we recommend Average on the ALC if you haven't got it there already.

a13_0551400.speaker: Lovell
a13_0551400.text: We're in Average, Jack.
